title: From Automated Simulation to Autonomous Discovery: A Hierarchical Framework for Agentic Computational Materials Science
authors: Linggang Zhu, Jian Zhou, Zhimei Sun
abstract: The convergence of large language models, materials-specific foundation models, and agentic artificial intelligence is reshaping the paradigm of computational materials discovery. While high-throughput computation, automated workflows, and data-driven modeling have greatly expanded the scale of materials exploration, the core scientific decision-making loop remains largely human-directed. Agentic AI introduces the possibility of systems that can autonomously reason about materials objectives, execute simulations, and refine strategies. However, the rapid emergence of such systems has created a critical need for a unified and operational framework to define, evaluate, and guide scientific autonomy in computational materials discovery. In this Perspective, we propose the Computational Materials Agent Autonomy Level (CMA-AL) framework, a hierarchical taxonomy defining six levels of autonomous agency in computational materials science: scripted excecutor, LLM-assisted operator, adaptive explorer, experiment-ready modeler, agentic digital twin, and self-extending intelligence. We further map emerging agentic systems onto the framework and identify key scientific and technological challenges toward higher autonomy. CMA-AL provides a common language for characterizing agentic computational materials discovery, evaluating the maturity of emerging systems, and guiding their evolution toward increasingly autonomous materials discovery.

infographic.key_insight: The paper proposes CMA-AL, a six-level hierarchy that formalizes how computational materials systems can progress from scripted workflows to self-extending autonomous discovery.
infographic.engineering_relevance: CMA-AL gives materials researchers and platform developers a shared benchmark for designing, comparing, and scaling agentic simulation pipelines toward more autonomous discovery.
method: Defines six autonomy levels: scripted executor, LLM-assisted operator, adaptive explorer, experiment-ready modeler, agentic digital twin, and self-extending intelligence.
Maps emerging agentic systems onto the hierarchy to assess current capability and maturity.
Uses the framework to identify scientific and technological gaps blocking higher autonomy.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract presents a perspective framework rather than new experimental datasets, and its support comes from taxonomy design plus conceptual mapping of existing agentic systems.
infographic.watch_item: A practical concern is that higher autonomy still depends on reliable evaluation, safety, and scientific validation, which are not yet standardized across materials platforms.
infographic.paper_title: From Automated Simulation to Autonomous Discovery: A Hierarchical Framework for Agentic Computational Materials Science

title: Co-PiLOT: Constrained Physics-Informed Latent Optimization for Target-Driven Inverse Design
authors: Mahish K. Guru, Mayank Nagar, Ayush vyas, Jan Bohlen, Roland Aydin, Noomane Ben Khalifa
abstract: Inverse design of physical systems (molecules, devices, microstructures) often reduces to optimizing a high-dimensional structure against an expensive black-box simulator. Direct search is difficult because the space is non-Euclidean, feasibility is hard to encode, and each evaluation is expensive. We present Co-PiLOT, a latent optimization approach that maps candidates through a generative encoder-decoder, uses the decoder as a learned validity prior, and searches the latent space with physics-informed black-box optimization. The framework is applied on the inverse design of magnesium alloy microstructure/texture. We develop a vision transformer based-encoder; paired with latent diffusion, diffusion transformer and rectified-flow transformer-based decoders on $\sim80{,}000$ EBSD-derived microstructure dataset to learn a minimal bottleneck, $z$. The ViT-FMDiT model ($z$=$768$) reconstructs high-fidelity microstructure images (FID $27.86$, MS-SSIM $0.178$), which our self-segmenting orientation codec converts into input grids for crystal plasticity solver. Finally, we introduce MERIDIAN, an active latent optimizer driven by deep-kernel Gaussian-process uncertainty, failure-aware feasibility prediction, manifold-aware trust regions, and target-aware acquisition. Within a budget of $160$ simulations, the ViT-FMDiT and MERIDIAN combination yields the best target-driven objective score, reducing the relative target error by $3$--$22\%$ against seven baselines (DANTE, TuRBO, BAxUS, CMA-ES, DDOM, SEIKO, DDPO) on the same decoder.

infographic.key_insight: Co-PiLOT turns inverse design into a constrained search in a learned latent space, using a generative decoder as a validity prior and a physics-informed optimizer to find target microstructures more efficiently.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This gives materials engineers a practical framework for designing magnesium alloy microstructures/texture with fewer expensive crystal-plasticity simulations while preserving feasibility.
method: Train a ViT-based encoder with latent diffusion, diffusion transformer, or rectified-flow transformer decoders to learn a compact microstructure latent space.
Use the decoder plus a self-segmenting orientation codec to map latent candidates into valid solver-ready EBSD-style inputs.
Optimize the latent codes with MERIDIAN: deep-kernel GP uncertainty, failure-aware feasibility prediction, manifold-aware trust regions, and target-aware acquisition.
infographic.evidence_signal: On an ~80,000-image EBSD-derived dataset, the ViT-FMDiT model with z=768 achieved FID 27.86 and MS-SSIM 0.178, and with 160 simulations outperformed seven baselines by reducing relative target error by 3–22%.
infographic.watch_item: The approach depends on a high-quality learned decoder and may be sensitive to distribution shift or reconstruction fidelity when transferring to new materials systems or processing conditions.
infographic.paper_title: Co-PiLOT: Constrained Physics-Informed Latent Optimization for Target-Driven Inverse Design

title: Linear-Scaling Quantum Transport from Machine-Learning Density Functional Theory Hamiltonians
authors: Bang Liu, Yang Zhong, Zhi-Xin Guo, Xin-Gao Gong, Hongjun Xiang
abstract: Quantum transport simulations that combine density functional theory (DFT) with the nonequilibrium Green's function formalism (DFT-NEGF) are important to modern technology, yet their unfavorable scaling has long confined predictive simulations to small, idealized systems far below the ten-thousand-atom scale of realistic devices. Here, we introduce HamGNN-NEGF, a linear-scaling framework with DFT-level fidelity. An E(3)-equivariant graph neural network trained on conventional DFT Hamiltonians of small structures predicts Hamiltonians for large devices, avoiding costly DFT-NEGF training data. The predicted Hamiltonians are integrated with DFT-derived electrode self-energies, a nonorthogonal kernel polynomial method for Fermi-level determination, and a recursive Green's function algorithm, yielding a computational cost that scales linearly with device length at fixed cross section. Even for devices containing fewer than 500 atoms, HamGNN-NEGF achieves speedups exceeding three orders of magnitude over fully self-consistent DFT-NEGF, with the advantage increasing further with system size. Benchmarks on pristine Pt-Si-Pt, doped Pt-Si:P-Pt, and Pt-molecule-Pt junctions demonstrate meV-level Hamiltonian accuracy, faithful transmission spectra, and predictive simulations beyond 10,000 atoms. Eliminating transport self-consistency also enables hybrid functionals such as HSE06 without additional NEGF overhead, while a zero-bias Hamiltonian approximation extends the framework to finite-bias transport in weakly nonlinear regimes. HamGNN-NEGF thus bridges first-principles accuracy and device-scale simulation, providing a practical route toward predictive modeling of realistic nanoelectronic and quantum devices.

infographic.key_insight: HamGNN-NEGF uses an E(3)-equivariant GNN to predict DFT-quality Hamiltonians for large devices, enabling linear-scaling quantum transport with near-DFT fidelity.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This makes predictive transport simulations feasible for realistic nanoelectronic devices at the 10,000-atom scale, far beyond conventional DFT-NEGF limits.
method: Train on conventional DFT Hamiltonians from small structures, not expensive DFT-NEGF data.
Predict device Hamiltonians with an E(3)-equivariant graph neural network.
Combine with DFT electrode self-energies, kernel polynomial Fermi-level estimation, and recursive Green's functions for linear scaling.
infographic.evidence_signal: Benchmarks on Pt-Si-Pt, doped Pt-Si:P-Pt, and Pt-molecule-Pt junctions report meV-level Hamiltonian accuracy, faithful transmission spectra, and >1000× speedups even below 500 atoms.
infographic.watch_item: The zero-bias Hamiltonian approximation is only expected to be reliable in weakly nonlinear regimes, so strong-bias transport may need additional validation.
infographic.paper_title: Linear-Scaling Quantum Transport from Machine-Learning Density Functional Theory Hamiltonians

title: Measuring trainable degrees of freedom in materials graph neural networks: a random-subspace intrinsic dimension analysis
authors: Shehroz Ahmad Shoaib, Kangming Li
abstract: Final predictive accuracy is the standard basis for comparing graph neural networks (GNNs) in materials-property prediction, but it does not show how strongly performance depends on access to trainable parameter-space directions. Here, we introduce trainable-degree dependence as a complementary characterization of materials GNN learning. Using random-subspace intrinsic-dimension analysis, we train CGCNN, ALIGNN, and DimeNet++ in randomly oriented parameter subspaces across six prediction tasks and measure how performance recovers as independent trainable degrees of freedom are restored. The resulting recovery curves separate endpoint accuracy from the trainable-dimensional demand required to recover it. They reveal distinctions that final errors alone miss: metallic classification and log-bulk-modulus regression recover near-reference performance from small fractional subspaces, formation-energy and band-gap prediction show stronger architecture dependence, and phonon prediction is most sensitive to dimensional restriction. Dataset-size sweeps show that band-gap models require larger fractional subspaces as training data grows, whereas formation-energy and bulk-modulus responses are more stable. A width sweep shows that fractional thresholds can remain stable while absolute threshold dimensions increase with model size. Random-subspace analysis therefore provides a targeted stress test for how materials GNNs use their optimization space.

infographic.key_insight: Materials GNNs can achieve similar final accuracy with very different amounts of trainable parameter-space freedom, so intrinsic dimensionality reveals a hidden measure of model dependence beyond endpoint error.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Random-subspace intrinsic-dimension analysis offers a practical stress test for choosing architectures and sizing models when robustness to reduced optimization capacity matters in materials property prediction.
method: Train CGCNN, ALIGNN, and DimeNet++ inside randomly oriented low-dimensional parameter subspaces.
Track recovery curves as more trainable degrees of freedom are restored.
Compare six prediction tasks plus dataset-size and width sweeps to separate accuracy from dimensional demand.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across six tasks, the authors report that metallic classification and log-bulk-modulus regression recover near-reference performance from small fractional subspaces, while phonon prediction is the most sensitive to dimensional restriction.
infographic.watch_item: Random-subspace results depend on the chosen architecture, task, and training setup, so threshold dimensions should be interpreted as comparative diagnostics rather than universal constants.
infographic.paper_title: Measuring trainable degrees of freedom in materials graph neural networks: a random-subspace intrinsic dimension analysis

title: A roadmap for polymer informatics super-intelligence
authors: Akhlak Mahmood, Janhavi Nistane, Huan Tran, Chiho Kim, Rampi Ramprasad
abstract: Polymer informatics has matured from isolated property-prediction studies into an integrated discipline that couples data, models, and decision-making across the polymer design cycle. Yet it still falls short of a true intelligent system capable of inverse design on demand, causal reasoning across chemistry, processing, and performance, and closed-loop autonomous experimentation. This article traces a roadmap toward that goal, grounded in experience developing two complementary agentic and informatics platforms. Central to this vision is a modular, agent-directed architecture in which a polymer super-intelligence layer interprets a researcher's design question in natural language and coordinates domain-specialized tools, matched to the available data, for neat polymers, composites and formulations, solvents, and synthesis and processing. The resulting system spans the full chain from molecular design through processing to product-level performance and human perception. Orchestrated together, its generative design, synthesis-feasibility reasoning, and practicality assessment already form the decision-making core of a self-driving polymer laboratory, leaving autonomous, closed-loop experimentation as the principal step that remains. We survey emerging capabilities along this roadmap, including automated extraction of property data from the literature, chemistry-aware representation, property prediction for membranes and sustainable plastics, solubility and green-solvent recommendation, and computer-guided retrosynthetic planning, exposing the remaining gaps and the research and infrastructure investments needed to move from today's orchestrated tool ecosystem toward a genuinely super-intelligent polymer design partner.

infographic.key_insight: The paper argues that polymer informatics is ready to evolve from isolated prediction tools into a modular, agentic super-intelligence that can interpret design goals, coordinate specialized models, and support end-to-end polymer discovery.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For computational materials engineering, this roadmap points toward AI systems that can accelerate inverse design, synthesis planning, process selection, and performance optimization across polymers, composites, solvents, and formulations.
method: Proposes a modular agent-directed architecture that maps a natural-language research question to domain-specific tools.
Covers the full design chain from molecular generation and property prediction to synthesis feasibility and practicality assessment.
Positions autonomous closed-loop experimentation as the remaining major step toward a self-driving polymer laboratory.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract cites experience building two complementary agentic and informatics platforms and surveys demonstrated capabilities across literature data extraction, chemistry-aware representation, property prediction, solvent recommendation, and retrosynthetic planning.
infographic.watch_item: The vision is still limited by gaps in autonomous closed-loop experimentation and by the need to match tools reliably to available data across diverse polymer classes and tasks.
infographic.paper_title: A roadmap for polymer informatics super-intelligence

title: Electronic Coupling and Charge-Transfer Landscape of Graphene on Ge(001)/Si(001): Multiscale Analysis Assisted by Machine Learning
authors: Pawel Dabrowski, Przemysław Przybysz, Maciej Rogala, Iaroslav Lutsyk, Paweł Krukowski, Witold Kozłowski
abstract: Understanding and controlling charge transfer at graphene-semiconductor interfaces is essential for the integration of two-dimensional materials into silicon-compatible technologies. Here, we combine ultraviolet photoelectron spectroscopy (UPS), Kelvin probe force microscopy (KPFM), angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES), scanning tunneling spectroscopy (STS) and density functional theory (DFT) to resolve work-function modulation and electronic coupling in graphene grown on Ge(001)/Si(001). UPS and KPFM reveal a spatially non-uniform work-function landscape correlated with the nanofaceted morphology of the substrate. ARPES and DFT calculations for the pristine interface consistently indicate n-type doping and electron transfer from Ge to graphene. In contrast, modeling of the oxidized interface predicts a reversal to p-type doping, providing a plausible explanation for the different doping polarities reported in the literature. Machine-learning-assisted classification of the STS data resolves distinct local electronic regimes, ranging from nearly free-standing graphene on nanofacet tops to more strongly coupled inter-facet regions and nanoribbon-like regions with distinct local electronic responses. By identifying the mechanisms governing local graphene-substrate interactions and charge transfer, our study provides guidelines for tailoring the synthesis process and minimizing defect formation during delamination. These insights support the production of high-quality graphene layers for electronic devices and for transfer as protective coatings for air-sensitive materials.

infographic.key_insight: Graphene on Ge(001)/Si(001) shows spatially varying electronic coupling and charge transfer that depends on the local nanofaceted interface, switching from n-type behavior in the pristine case to p-type under oxidation.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Understanding and controlling this interfacial doping landscape helps optimize graphene integration with silicon-compatible platforms and improve graphene transfer quality for device and protective-coating applications.
method: UPS and KPFM mapped work-function variations across the nanofaceted surface.
ARPES and DFT compared pristine versus oxidized interfaces to determine doping polarity.
STS data were classified with machine learning to separate local electronic regimes.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports consistent agreement between spectroscopy and DFT, plus ML-resolved STS regimes spanning nearly free-standing, strongly coupled, and nanoribbon-like regions.
infographic.watch_item: The oxidation state and local morphology strongly affect the observed doping, so interface preparation and environmental control are critical for reproducible device behavior.
infographic.paper_title: Electronic Coupling and Charge-Transfer Landscape of Graphene on Ge(001)/Si(001): Multiscale Analysis Assisted by Machine Learning

title: MatToolBench: Benchmarking Multimodal Agents in Real-World Materials Science Workflows
authors: Mei Wu, Rui Xie, Runyu Zhang, Yuqiang Li, Tianfan Fu, Bo Chen
abstract: Multimodal GUI agents have achieved impressive results on general software benchmarks, yet their ability to operate professional scientific software remains largely unexplored. In materials science, sparse domain-specific web data, specialized interfaces, and tacit workflow conventions create blind spots that general-purpose pretraining cannot readily bridge. We present MatToolBench, the first real-environment benchmark for evaluating multimodal GUI agents on professional materials science software, comprising 204 tasks across 10 tools in three modalities: GUI operation, OriginPro scripting, and code-based database queries, all executed inside a Windows 11 VM. Each task is decomposed into fine-grained sub-criteria by domain experts, enabling interpretable partial-credit scoring; the GUI component of our multi-level evaluation pipeline achieves an average F1 of 0.98. For OriginPro figure-generation tasks, we further conduct a human-LLM agreement study to validate the use of a multimodal judge for secondary aesthetic assessment. Our experiments show that strong performance on general benchmarks does not transfer to professional scientific workflows, and that this gap is not a visual-grounding problem alone: failures arise from domain-specific operational knowledge, sparse pretraining coverage of scientific software, weak cross-tool artifact handoff, and critical states exposed only visually. Even the best model reaches only 25% success rate on GUI tasks and 45% on code tasks. MatToolBench therefore serves as a challenging diagnostic benchmark and real-environment testbed for data-scarce, knowledge-intensive scientific workflows.

infographic.key_insight: MatToolBench shows that multimodal agents that excel on general software benchmarks still struggle badly with real materials-science workflows because the bottlenecks are domain knowledge, tool-specific conventions, and cross-tool coordination—not just visual grounding.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The benchmark gives engineers a realistic way to measure and improve AI assistants for scientific software, script-driven analysis, and database querying in materials research.
method: Built a real-environment benchmark with 204 tasks spanning 10 materials-science tools in three modes: GUI操作, OriginPro scripting, and code-based database queries.
Executed tasks inside a Windows 11 VM and used expert-defined sub-criteria for partial-credit scoring.
Validated a multimodal judge for OriginPro figure aesthetics with a human-LLM agreement study.
infographic.evidence_signal: The evaluation pipeline reports an average GUI scoring F1 of 0.98, while the strongest model achieved only 25% success on GUI tasks and 45% on code tasks.
infographic.watch_item: Results may depend on the specific Windows 11 VM setup and the limited tool set, so transfer to other scientific software stacks should be tested carefully.
infographic.paper_title: MatToolBench: Benchmarking Multimodal Agents in Real-World Materials Science Workflows

title: Where Should Physics Enter a Molecular Crystal Generator?
authors: Haocheng Tang, Junmei Wang, Wengong Jin
abstract: Generative models make molecular crystal structure prediction fast, but their samples still exhibit geometric and packing violations. Physics can be introduced during training, post-training, or inference, yet these choices are rarely compared with the generator and physical signal held fixed. We introduce CrystAF, an all-atom crystal flow-map generation model, and use it with the UMA interatomic potential to systematically study where physics should enter. Post-training learns physical preferences directly into CrystAF, improving molecular validity and crystal packing while leaving sampling unchanged: physics is paid for once during training rather than repeatedly at deployment. In contrast, UMA relaxation is effective at repairing local clashes but makes generation 6--26$\times$ slower, while learning from relaxed targets provides little benefit. These routes are complementary rather than competing. Physics-informed post-training first shifts the generated distribution toward more physically reasonable structures, after which inexpensive inference-time corrections further remove clashes and restore stereochemistry that the generator cannot represent. Importantly, the same post-training strategy also improves the multi-step all-atom Clari-M and rigid-body MolCrystalFlow generators, demonstrating transfer across architectures and representations. Together, our results suggest a simple principle: learn reusable physical alignment into the generator, and reserve inference-time physics for residual constraints that are better corrected than learned.

infographic.key_insight: Physics is most effective when learned once during training, with inference-time corrections reserved for residual geometric issues that the generator cannot easily represent.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For molecular crystal generation, post-training with physical signals improves validity and packing without slowing deployment, while runtime relaxation can fix clashes but incurs a large speed penalty.
method: Built CrystAF, an all-atom crystal flow-map generator.
Compared three physics-integration points: during training, after training, and at inference using the UMA interatomic potential.
Tested transfer of the same post-training strategy to Clari-M and MolCrystalFlow.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports that post-training improves molecular validity and crystal packing, UMA relaxation slows generation by 6–26×, and the approach generalizes across multiple generator architectures.
infographic.watch_item: Inference-time relaxation can repair local clashes, but over-reliance on it may be expensive and cannot fully replace learning physically aligned structure priors.
infographic.paper_title: Where Should Physics Enter a Molecular Crystal Generator?

title: Density functional perturbation theory of meta-generalized gradient approximations using algorithmic differentiation
authors: Bruno Ploumhans, Niklas Frederik Schmitz, Michael F. Herbst
abstract: Density functional perturbation theory (DFPT) is an established framework for the computation of derivatives in plane-wave density functional theory. We present an implementation of DFPT for exchange-correlation (XC) functionals $E_\mathrm{xc}(ρ,τ)$ that incorporate an explicit dependence on both the density $ρ$ and the kinetic energy density $τ$. This covers the popular class of semilocal meta-generalized gradient approximations (meta-GGAs) as well as broader nonlocal parametrizations. We sidestep the derivation of cumbersome XC second energy derivative expressions by recasting these derivatives as a Jacobian-vector product of the XC potentials, which we evaluate with algorithmic differentiation (AD) techniques. Integration with our previously developed AD-DFPT framework [N. F. Schmitz et al., npj Comput. Mater. 12, 6 (2026)] provides access to derivatives of arbitrary ground state quantities with respect to arbitrary perturbations. We employ AD-DFPT to compute a range of response properties for ZnO and BaTiO3, and find that the recent r2SCAN01 meta-GGA functional generally outperforms LDA and PBE. Finally, we showcase the optimization of a neural-network meta-GGA to self-consistently reproduce hybrid-DFT reference densities of bulk silicon, using AD-DFPT gradients. Overall, these results establish AD-DFPT as a versatile route for computing DFT derivatives at the meta-GGA level, be they common response properties or the unusual derivatives required for the gradient-based training of novel XC functionals.

infographic.key_insight: AD-DFPT can compute meta-GGA density-functional response derivatives by using algorithmic differentiation to avoid manual second-derivative XC formulas.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This makes advanced DFT response calculations and gradient-based functional training more practical for materials modeling workflows.
method: Recast XC second derivatives as Jacobian-vector products of the XC potentials.
Use algorithmic differentiation within an AD-DFPT framework.
Apply the approach to meta-GGA functionals such as r2SCAN01 and to neural-network XC optimization.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports response-property calculations for ZnO and BaTiO3 and an optimization task on bulk silicon, with r2SCAN01 generally outperforming LDA and PBE.
infographic.watch_item: Accuracy and robustness depend on correct AD implementation and self-consistent convergence for meta-GGA XC terms, which can be more complex than standard GGA cases.
infographic.paper_title: Density functional perturbation theory of meta-generalized gradient approximations using algorithmic differentiation

title: Accelerating phase-field simulations on exascale computing systems for faster-than-real-time precipitate aging predictions
authors: Stephen DeWitt, David J. Gardner, Philip Fackler, Yonggil Song, Miroslav Stoyanov, Carol S. Woodward
abstract: Three-dimensional phase-field simulations are a gold-standard for microstructure prediction for materials, but their computational cost often limits application-relevant calculations to modest domain sizes and timescales. Here, we present a holistic approach for accelerating Fourier pseudospectral phase-field simulations by combining performance-portable GPU computing, large-scale distributed-memory parallelism, and high-order implicit-explicit time integration within the MEUMAPPS C++ framework. We demonstrate this approach with a 1.5-billion-grid-point simulation of the growth and coarsening of 1,920 gamma'' precipitates in a Ni-Nb-Fe alloy. The simulated seven-hour heat treatment is completed in 5.5 hours, making the calculation faster than real time and an estimated 217-501x faster than a CPU-only, first-order baseline. This performance makes three-dimensional simulations of thousands of interacting precipitates tractable, enabling quantitative studies ocollective microstructural phenomena, large simulation ensembles, and real-time integration into controlling and interpreting experiments. Benchmarking shows single-node GPU speedups of up to 17.5x relative to comparable CPU resources, near-ideal strong scaling to 4096 GPUs for a 12-billion-grid-point problem, and a further 2.6-2.9x acceleration from fourth-order time integration at scientifically relevant error tolerances. These results establish a performance-portable strategy for exploiting leadership-scale GPU systems that is applicable to a broad class of Fourier pseudospectral simulations beyond phase-field models such as fluid dynamics and crystal plasticity simulations.

infographic.key_insight: A performance-portable GPU + distributed-memory + high-order time-integration strategy makes large 3D phase-field precipitate simulations faster than real time.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This enables application-scale microstructure prediction for materials design, large simulation ensembles, and potential real-time support for experiments on exascale systems.
method: Used MEUMAPPS C++ with performance-portable GPU computing and large-scale distributed-memory parallelism.
Applied Fourier pseudospectral phase-field simulation with high-order implicit-explicit time integration.
Demonstrated on a 1.5-billion-grid-point Ni-Nb-Fe precipitate aging case.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports a seven-hour heat treatment completed in 5.5 hours, up to 17.5x single-node GPU speedup, near-ideal strong scaling to 4096 GPUs, and 2.6–2.9x gain from fourth-order time integration.
infographic.watch_item: Performance gains may depend on access to leadership-class GPU systems and careful tuning of solver accuracy, communication, and memory traffic.
infographic.paper_title: Accelerating phase-field simulations on exascale computing systems for faster-than-real-time precipitate aging predictions

title: Pressure-induced s,p-d electron redistribution accompanies structural transformation in amorphous Zr-Cu alloy under compression
authors: P. Dziegielewski, J. Antonowicz, K. Georgarakis, O. Lord, M. Amboage, D. Daisenberger
abstract: Extreme compression can reorganize atomic valence states, in some regimes driving charge from spatially extended orbitals into more compact ones. We investigate this effect in amorphous Zr67Cu33 metallic glass by combining high-pressure X-ray absorption fine structure measurements up to 69 GPa with molecular dynamics simulations and density functional theory calculations. The Zr K-edge XANES spectra show a pronounced increase in the pre-edge intensity and a change in its pressure dependence, whereas the Cu response is markedly weaker. Molecular-dynamics simulations reproduce the measured EXAFS spectra and provide reliable input for the electronic-structure calculations. The calculated Mulliken populations reveal pressure-induced depletion of Zr s and p-states, accompanied by an increase of the d-state population, while the density of states indicates enhanced p-d hybridization under compression. These results provide experimental and computational evidence for pressure-induced s,p-d electronic redistribution in zirconium and link this effect to the previously reported anomalous structural evolution of the compressed amorphous alloy.

infographic.key_insight: Under strong compression, amorphous Zr67Cu33 undergoes a pressure-driven electronic redistribution: Zr loses s,p character and gains d character, accompanied by stronger p–d hybridization.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This suggests pressure can tune bonding and structural evolution in metallic glasses, which is relevant for designing high-strength, compression-resistant amorphous alloys.
method: High-pressure X-ray absorption fine structure measurements up to 69 GPa
Molecular dynamics simulations to reproduce EXAFS spectra
Density functional theory to analyze Mulliken populations and density of states
infographic.evidence_signal: The Zr K-edge XANES shows a pronounced pre-edge intensity increase and altered pressure dependence, while simulations reproduce EXAFS and electronic-structure calculations confirm s,p to d redistribution.
infographic.watch_item: The main conclusions rely on combining experiment with simulations and electronic-structure models, so quantitative interpretation may depend on the accuracy of the amorphous-structure model and pressure conditions.
infographic.paper_title: Pressure-induced s,p-d electron redistribution accompanies structural transformation in amorphous Zr-Cu alloy under compression

title: Assessing the Transferability of General-Purpose MachineLearning Interatomic Potentials for Heterogeneous Catalysis with HetCat26
authors: Alexandre Peuch, Giaan Kler-Young, Kaifeng Niu, Jinwoo Hwang, Manos Mavrikakis, Angelos Michaelides
abstract: Foundation machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) promise near-density functional theory (DFT) accuracy across broad areas of chemistry and materials science. However, their performance in describing systems and processes relevant to heterogeneous catalysis remains underexplored. Here, we introduce HetCat26, a collection of benchmark tests designed to assess pre-trained MLIPs across key aspects of catalytic modeling, including surface energetics, metal-metal oxide interactions, adsorption, and catalytic reaction networks. Evaluating fifteen foundation models, we find that performance on existing general materials benchmarks is only weakly predictive of performance on HetCat26; transferability to heterogeneous catalysis cannot be inferred from these general benchmarks. Across the benchmark tests, current models describe surface energetics and, perhaps surprisingly, reaction barriers well, whereas larger errors are observed for adsorption, and DFT site preferences are often not reproduced. Two models, eSEN-30M-OAM and MACE-MH-1-OMAT, nevertheless achieve high accuracy across the properties evaluated. Beyond model benchmarking, HetCat26 highlights the importance of training data consistency: PBE and PBE+U calculations should not be mixed within a training set. Overall, we identify challenges limiting the transferability of current foundation MLIPs to heterogeneous catalysis and, more broadly, to chemical reactions at interfaces, providing guidance for the development of the next generation of foundation models.

infographic.key_insight: Existing general-purpose ML interatomic potentials do not reliably transfer to heterogeneous catalysis, so catalysis-specific benchmarking is needed to judge real predictive value.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For catalyst design and screening, these models can be useful for surface energetics and some barriers, but adsorption and site preferences still need careful validation against DFT.
method: Built HetCat26, a benchmark suite for heterogeneous catalysis covering surfaces, metal/oxide interactions, adsorption, and reaction networks.
Evaluated 15 pre-trained foundation MLIPs against catalysis-specific tests.
Compared performance on HetCat26 with broader materials benchmarks and training-data consistency effects.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across HetCat26, the study found good performance for surface energetics and some reaction barriers, but larger errors for adsorption and frequent failures to reproduce DFT site preferences; two models stood out as consistently accurate.
infographic.watch_item: Do not mix PBE and PBE+U data in the same training set, as inconsistent reference data can degrade transferability and benchmarking reliability.
infographic.paper_title: Assessing the Transferability of General-Purpose MachineLearning Interatomic Potentials for Heterogeneous Catalysis with HetCat26

title: Polar-Domain Volume as a Unified Descriptor of Transport in Ionic Liquids
authors: Ganesh K. Rajahmundry, Tarak K. Patra
abstract: Developing molecular scale structural descriptors that can quantitatively predict the macroscopic transport properties of ionic liquids remains a longstanding question, owing to the complex interplay between molecular interactions, nanoscale organization, and collective ion dynamics. Here, we use all atom molecular dynamics simulations to establish quantitative structure property relationships between the equilibrium microstructure and two key transport properties viscosity and ionic conductivity in a series of imidazolium based ILs with chemically distinct anions and varying alkyl chain lengths. While viscosity and ionic conductivity exhibit distinct dependencies on alkyl chain length and anion chemistry, these seemingly different trends largely collapse onto unified correlations when expressed in terms of the mean polar-domain volume. In particular, both transport properties exhibit systematic power-law scaling with the mean polar domain volume fraction, revealing a common structural origin underlying the variations in ion and momentum transport across chemically distinct ILs. These results establish polar-domain volume as a physically motivated molecular-scale descriptor and provide a general structure property framework for connecting nanoscale organization to macroscopic transport properties in ILs.

infographic.key_insight: The mean polar-domain volume in imidazolium ionic liquids unifies two seemingly different transport trends—viscosity and ionic conductivity—into a common structure–property scaling law.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This descriptor offers a physically grounded way to screen and design ionic liquids with targeted flow and charge-transport behavior from molecular structure alone.
method: All-atom molecular dynamics simulations of imidazolium-based ionic liquids.
Compared transport properties across different anions and alkyl-chain lengths.
Correlated viscosity and ionic conductivity with mean polar-domain volume fraction using power-law scaling.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports quantitative structure–property correlations across a chemically diverse set of ionic liquids, with both viscosity and ionic conductivity collapsing onto unified power-law trends versus polar-domain volume.
infographic.watch_item: The descriptor is validated on a specific imidazolium IL set, so broader generalization to other cation families or conditions will need additional testing.
infographic.paper_title: Polar-Domain Volume as a Unified Descriptor of Transport in Ionic Liquids

title: Bounding Retraining Equivalence and the Deletion Floor in Materials Machine Unlearning
authors: Can Polat, Mustafa Kurban, Erchin Serpedin, Hasan Kurban
abstract: In materials machine learning, closely related retained structures can sustain accurate property predictions even after removing a specific record, rendering post-deletion prediction error an ambiguous metric for machine unlearning. To resolve this ambiguity, we define the deletion floor as the expected target loss under a specified retraining procedure at the deleted request. Standard indistinguishability constraints yield a sharp interval bounding an update's target loss around this baseline reference. Theoretically, a conditional neighbor bound links a low deletion floor directly to retained fit, prediction regularity, and local label agreement, while an exact ridge identity isolates residual fit from the prediction change induced by record deletion. Empirically, controlled redundancy sweeps show an $\approx 8\times$ drop in median normalized retraining loss when one retained relative remains after deletion. Across two distinct fitting regimes in a paired Materials Project study, the lower-floor regime also exhibits a larger prediction change on more than 50% of the shared requests. Systematic comparisons against approximate updates and the original model decouple deliberate target suppression from preserved overall model utility. Consequently, request-level unlearning evaluations should report reference loss, prediction change, and retained utility together, interpreting post-deletion accuracy against what retraining itself leaves behind.

infographic.key_insight: Post-deletion accuracy alone can be misleading for materials machine unlearning, so the paper defines a “deletion floor” as the retraining loss baseline and bounds how much a deletion update can deviate from it.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For property prediction models in materials science, unlearning should be judged relative to what retraining leaves behind, not just by whether the deleted sample is hard to predict.
method: Defines the deletion floor: expected target loss under a specified retraining procedure at the deleted request.
Derives sharp indistinguishability-based bounds on an update’s target loss around that baseline.
Provides a conditional neighbor bound and an exact ridge identity linking retrained fit, prediction regularity, and deletion-induced change.
infographic.evidence_signal: Experiments report an approximately 8× drop in median normalized retraining loss when one retained relative remains after deletion, and a paired Materials Project study shows the lower-floor regime has larger prediction changes on more than 50% of shared requests.
infographic.watch_item: The deletion floor depends on the chosen retraining procedure, so comparisons across methods must keep the retraining reference and evaluation protocol consistent.
infographic.paper_title: Bounding Retraining Equivalence and the Deletion Floor in Materials Machine Unlearning

title: GLASS: Global Latent Aggregation with Slot-based Set Decoding for Scalable All-Atom Crystal Generation
authors: Hendrik Kraß, Seyed Mohamad Moosavi, Mathias Niepert
abstract: Generative models for crystals enable the discovery of novel structures, but scaling all-atom generation to larger systems such as metal--organic frameworks remains challenging. We connect this difficulty to the correspondence problem of particle-space generation. Even on a single fixed target set, index-free permutation-equivariant particle flows require substantially more training for reliable generation as set size and density increase, under both independent and optimal-transport couplings. To resolve this challenge, we introduce GLASS---Global Latent Aggregation with Slot-based Set Decoding, which encodes structures in a permutation-invariant global latent space and learns their distribution via flow matching. A learned-slot decoder constructs all atoms in parallel, removing atom-wise correspondence from generative transport. On MP20, GLASS is competitive with particle-space models, and flow training can reach the validity of the training data at every structure size. On a QMOF subset, GLASS generates MOFs with up to 150 atoms per unit cell without conditioning on building blocks, topology, or composition, and approaches the structural validity of the training data. On both datasets, flow training exposes a validity--novelty tradeoff, and MOF novelty remains limited by autoencoder generalization on the available data. These results show that separating correspondence assignment from generative transport provides a simple route toward high-validity generation of larger atomistic systems.

infographic.key_insight: GLASS improves scalable all-atom crystal generation by moving correspondence handling out of the generative flow: it learns a permutation-invariant global latent and uses slot-based parallel decoding to build atoms without atom-wise transport.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This makes generation of larger crystals and MOFs more practical, especially when atom counts grow and particle-space methods struggle with reliability and training cost.
method: Encode each structure into a permutation-invariant global latent space.
Train the latent distribution with flow matching.
Decode atoms in parallel with learned slots, avoiding index-based correspondence during generation.
infographic.evidence_signal: On MP20, GLASS matches particle-space baselines and reaches the validity of the training data across structure sizes; on a QMOF subset, it generates MOFs with up to 150 atoms per unit cell and approaches training-data validity.
infographic.watch_item: Novelty is constrained by a validity–novelty tradeoff, and MOF novelty is further limited by the autoencoder’s generalization on the available data.
infographic.paper_title: GLASS: Global Latent Aggregation with Slot-based Set Decoding for Scalable All-Atom Crystal Generation

title: How Thermodynamically Accessible are Quaternary Mixed-Metal Chalcohalides?
authors: Pascal Henkel, G. Krishnamurthy Grandhi, Jarno Laakso, David Rovira Ferrer, Edgardo Saucedo, Jingrui Li
abstract: Quaternary mixed-metal chalcohalides (MMCHs) are a promising mixed-anion semiconductor family, but their thermodynamic accessibility remains largely unexplored. We combine density functional theory with the Alexandria Materials Database to carry out a rapid and reliable evaluation of the thermodynamic accessibility of 54 M(II)$_2$M(III)Ch$_2$X$_3$ compounds. All evaluated MMCHs are predicted to be thermodynamically unstable, but a considerable fraction of MMCHs lie within computational uncertainty of the convex hull. Their predicted decomposition follows five distinct reaction pathways, most commonly into M(III)$_2$Ch$_3$, M(II)X$_2$, and M(II)Ch. Solution processing of six Sn-based MMCHs supports our analysis. Notably, this includes the first synthesis of the previously unreported Sn$_2$InS$_2$Br$_3$ in a multiphase film. Our approach identifies convex hull proximity and competing phase formation as key constraints on MMCH synthetic accessibility during solution processing, thereby guiding future MMCH exploration.

infographic.key_insight: All 54 evaluated quaternary mixed-metal chalcohalides are thermodynamically unstable, but many sit close enough to the convex hull to remain plausible synthesis targets.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For solution-processing workflows, convex-hull proximity and likely competing phases can be used to prioritize which mixed-anion semiconductors are worth attempting first.
method: DFT stability calculations for 54 M(II)2M(III)Ch2X3 compounds
Cross-referenced predictions with the Alexandria Materials Database
Compared predicted decomposition pathways against experimental solution-processing results
infographic.evidence_signal: The study combines density functional theory with database screening and experimental validation on six Sn-based compounds, including first synthesis of Sn2InS2Br3 in a multiphase film.
infographic.watch_item: Computational uncertainty near the hull means apparent accessibility may not translate into clean phase-pure synthesis, especially when multiple competing phases are present.
infographic.paper_title: How Thermodynamically Accessible are Quaternary Mixed-Metal Chalcohalides?

title: Study of LAGP coating on polyethylene separator for polysulfide suppression in thin Li-S batteries
authors: Giovanni Ceccio, Jiri Vacik
abstract: The use of a thin solid electrolyte layer on polyethylene (PE) separators has been explored as a potential strategy to mitigate the polysulfide shuttle effect in lithium-sulfur (Li-S) batteries, a phenomenon responsible for significantly reducing their lifespan. While some solid electrolytes, such as LAGP , have demonstrated the ability to effectively suppress the shuttle effect, their brittle ceramic nature limits their application, particularly in flexible electronics. Coating PE separators with LAGP nanofilms offers a promising solution by combining the mechanical flexibility and thinness of polymer separators with the electrochemical advantages of LAGP, due to its NASICON-like structure and high ionic conductivity. In this study, PE separators were coated with LAGP nanofilms using the ion sputtering technique and further modified with ferroic elements such as Ni and Co. The surface morphology of the coated separators was analyzed using scanning electron microscopy (SEM), and staircase voltammetry was employed to evaluate the electrochemical performance and modifications induced by the coatings. The results demonstrate that the use of PE separators with a thin LAGP layer significantly influences polysulfide diffusion and suppresses the shuttle effect, thereby reducing unwanted processes in Li-S batteries.

infographic.key_insight: A thin LAGP coating on a polyethylene separator can reduce polysulfide shuttle in thin Li-S batteries while preserving the separator’s flexibility.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This approach offers a practical separator-coating route to improve Li-S battery durability without replacing polymer separators with brittle ceramics.
method: Ion-sputtered LAGP nanofilms were deposited on polyethylene separators.
Some coatings were further modified with Ni and Co ferroic elements.
SEM and staircase voltammetry were used to assess morphology and electrochemical behavior.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports that LAGP-coated PE separators significantly influenced polysulfide diffusion and suppressed shuttle-related processes in Li-S batteries.
infographic.watch_item: The ceramic coating may still pose integration challenges for flexible devices, especially if uniform thin-film coverage or mechanical robustness is insufficient.
infographic.paper_title: Study of LAGP coating on polyethylene separator for polysulfide suppression in thin Li-S batteries

title: High-Throughput Imaging of Degradation-Inducing Microscopic Impurities in Perovskite Solar Cells
authors: Sofiia Kosar, Anil R. Pininti, Vladyslav Hnapovskyi, José P. Jurado, Subhashri Mannar, Lorenzo Mardegan
abstract: The scalable fabrication of high-quality, large-area perovskite thin films is hindered by microscopic inhomogeneities, particularly residual compositional impurities formed during processing. Identifying these impurities, understanding their impact on device operation, and enabling their rapid detection are essential for upscaling perovskite solar cells (PSCs). Here, nano-Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy combined with high-resolution optical and scanning probe techniques was used to identify detrimental impurities in wide-bandgap perovskite films relevant to tandem solar cells. Photo-stress experiments revealed that degradation of the perovskite layer initiates at impurity-perovskite interfaces, demonstrating that impurities act as failure nucleation sites. Leveraging these insights, a rapid, non-invasive, and high-throughput framework based on high-resolution reflected light microscopy and machine learning-supported image analysis was developed, enabling detection and quantification of harmful impurities in as-prepared films within seconds. Films with higher impurity density show accelerated early degradation, establishing this parameter as an early-warning metric for stability screening. Extending this framework to degradation tracking further reveals coupled photo- and thermo-chemical contributions to impurity-mediated instability. Overall, this work establishes a practical chemically-validated diagnostic imaging framework for rapid pre-screening of perovskite films to enable stable and scalable PSCs.

infographic.key_insight: Microscopic residual impurities in wide-bandgap perovskite films act as degradation nucleation sites, and can be rapidly detected with microscopy plus machine learning.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This enables fast, non-invasive pre-screening of perovskite thin films to improve reliability and scalability for solar-cell manufacturing.
method: Nano-FTIR spectroscopy chemically identified harmful impurities.
High-resolution reflected-light microscopy captured impurity patterns.
Machine-learning image analysis quantified impurity density within seconds.
infographic.evidence_signal: Photo-stress experiments showed degradation starts at impurity–perovskite interfaces, and films with higher impurity density degraded faster early on.
infographic.watch_item: The imaging workflow should be chemically validated on each film stack and may need recalibration across processing recipes, compositions, and microscope setups.
infographic.paper_title: High-Throughput Imaging of Degradation-Inducing Microscopic Impurities in Perovskite Solar Cells

title: Physics-Guided Conditional Diffusion Model for Rare Event Synthesis and Diagnosis for the Water-Gas Shift Reaction
authors: Md Abrar Rafid Siddique, Bibek Aryal, Qiugang Lu
abstract: As the world moves towards sustainable energy sources, hydrogen (H2) can be treated as an eco-friendly alternative to fossil fuels due to its high energy density and zero carbon emissions. The water-gas shift (WGS) reaction is a widely used industrial process for hydrogen production by converting carbon monoxide and steam into hydrogen and carbon dioxide. However, occurrences like severe fouling, catalyst deterioration, and thermal runaway can hamper the reaction kinetics/process safety and decrease the yield of H2. These incidents are rare, and gathering process data under such abnormal conditions is challenging. In this work, we propose a physics-guided conditional diffusion model to generate realistic rare-event trajectories for the WGS reaction. The proposed model integrates a conditional denoising diffusion probabilistic model (CDDPM) with governing laws of the reaction to generate physically consistent process trajectories. The conditioning features allow the model to produce high-quality synthetic profiles for rare-event domains that are typically beyond the training regimes. The generated rare-event trajectories then augment the raw dataset for a balanced distribution between normal and abnormal conditions. We further propose a hazard score to assess the risk severity of the operating condition based on the operating trajectory. Deep learning models are trained with the augmented dataset to diagnose the health status of the reaction. Simulation results show that the proposed physics-guided diffusion model outperforms data-driven models in terms of the quality of synthetic data and diagnosis performance for rare events.

infographic.key_insight: A physics-guided conditional diffusion model can synthesize realistic rare-event water-gas shift trajectories, enabling better fault diagnosis when abnormal process data are scarce.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This approach helps improve hydrogen-production process safety and reliability by augmenting rare abnormal-condition data for monitoring and early warning.
method: Conditioned diffusion model generates rare-event process trajectories beyond the normal training regime.
Physics guidance embeds reaction governing laws to keep synthetic profiles physically consistent.
Augmented data are used to train diagnosis models and a hazard score ranks operating-risk severity.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports that simulations show the physics-guided diffusion model produces higher-quality synthetic data and better rare-event diagnosis than data-driven baselines.
infographic.watch_item: Performance may depend on the quality of the embedded physics assumptions and how well the model generalizes to unseen operating conditions.
infographic.paper_title: Physics-Guided Conditional Diffusion Model for Rare Event Synthesis and Diagnosis for the Water-Gas Shift Reaction

title: Disentangling octahedral distortion and symmetry breaking in the ordered double perovskite SrLaCoNbO$_6$
authors: Ajay Kumar, Clemens Ulrich, Yaroslav Mudryk, Rajendra S. Dhaka
abstract: We report a comprehensive high temperature structural investigation of the B-site ordered double perovskite SrLaCoNbO$_6$ using combined Raman spectroscopy and x-ray diffraction (XRD) over the range 25--900~$^\circ$C. Two distinct temperature-driven anomalies are identified at $T_\mathrm{OD} = 300\pm 25~^\circ$C and $T_\mathrm{PT} = 750\pm 25~^\circ$C through pronounced renormalizations in the phonon frequency and linewidth, accompanied by the evolution and suppression of characteristic XRD reflections. The low-temperature anomaly at $T_\mathrm{OD}$ is associated with an isostructural octahedral distortion within the monoclinic $P2_1/n$ phase. At $T_\mathrm{OD}$, the radial and angular distortion parameters of the CoO$_6$ and NbO$_6$ octahedra decrease to near-zero values before reversing upon further heating due to an inversion of the in-plane Co--O and Nb--O bond-length hierarchy. The high-temperature anomaly at $T_\mathrm{PT}$ corresponds to a symmetry-breaking structural phase transition from $P2_1/n$ to the monoclinic $I2/m$ phase, confirmed by group-theoretical analysis and Rietveld refinement. These results demonstrate that integrating temperature-dependent Raman spectroscopy with laboratory-based XRD, complemented by quantitative octahedral distortion analysis, provides a robust approach to disentangle isostructural octahedral distortions from symmetry-breaking phase transitions in complex double perovskite oxides without recourse to synchrotron or neutron diffraction facilities.

infographic.key_insight: Temperature-dependent Raman and XRD separate two distinct structural events in SrLaCoNbO6: a low-temperature isostructural octahedral distortion near 300 °C and a higher-temperature symmetry-breaking transition near 750 °C.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The study provides a practical lab-scale workflow to diagnose functional structure changes in ordered double perovskites, helping guide thermal stability, phase-control, and defect-structure design.
method: Combined Raman spectroscopy and laboratory XRD from 25–900 °C
Tracked phonon frequency/linewidth renormalization and XRD peak evolution
Quantified octahedral distortion parameters and used group-theoretical/Rietveld analysis
infographic.evidence_signal: Two anomalies were observed at T_OD = 300±25 °C and T_PT = 750±25 °C, supported by phonon renormalization, suppression/evolution of characteristic XRD reflections, and refinement-based phase assignment.
infographic.watch_item: The transition temperatures are approximate and the structural interpretation depends on careful peak indexing and distortion analysis, so similar signatures in related perovskites may require cross-validation.
infographic.paper_title: Disentangling octahedral distortion and symmetry breaking in the ordered double perovskite SrLaCoNbO$_6$
